sections.title: 1. Process vs. Thread Anatomy
sections.description: What a process owns, what threads share, and what each thread keeps private.

blocks.title: Anatomy of a Process & Its Address Space
blocks.content:
A **process** (*processus*) is an independent program in execution managed by the operating system. Every process owns:

* Compiled executable code (**Text segment**)
* Its own isolated **address space** (*espace d'adressage*)
* A **priority** and a unique **identifier (PID)**
* An **execution context** (Program Counter `PC` + CPU registers)

### Memory Layout of a Process

| Segment | Purpose | Shared Across Threads? |
| :--- | :--- | :---: |
| **Stack segment** (*pile*) | Procedure call frames, return addresses, local variables | **No** — each thread gets its own stack |
| **Data segment** (*tas / heap* & globals) | Global variables (`static`, globals) and dynamic allocations (`new`, `malloc`) | **Yes** — shared by all threads of the process |
| **Text segment** | Compiled machine instructions to execute | **Yes** — shared (read-only) |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Key Distinction:** Each thread has its **own stack** and **own execution context** (`PC`, `SP`, registers), but **all threads within the same process share the same address space** (Data + Text segments). Threads of *different* processes do **not** share an address space.

blocks.title: Processes vs. Threads: Communication & Control
blocks.content:
| Aspect | Process (*Processus*) | Thread |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Address Space** | Own isolated address space | **Shared** within the same process |
| **Inter-task Communication** | Requires OS IPC mechanisms (pipes, sockets, shared memory) | Direct: read/write shared global or heap variables |
| **Peer Control** | Child processes cannot control sibling processes or the parent | All threads of a process are **peers**: any thread can control another (or the main thread, affecting the whole process) |
| **Creation Cost** | Heavy (new address space, OS tables) | Light (shares existing address space; only needs a new stack & context) |

sections.title: 2. Thread Lifecycle, Context Switch & Thread Models
sections.description: The 5-state lifecycle diagram, single-core vs. multi-core execution, and green vs. native threads.

blocks.title: States and Transitions of a Thread
blocks.content:
A thread's lifecycle closely mirrors that of a Unix process:

1. **Prêt (*Ready*):** Eligible to run, waiting for a CPU core. Entered upon creation, wake-up (*réveil*), or preemption.
2. **Élu (*Running*):** Currently executing instructions on a CPU core.
   * On a **single-core CPU** (*monocœur*), at most **1** thread is in the *élu* state at any instant (**min 0, max 1**—0 if all threads are blocked or idle).
   * On a **multi-core CPU** with $k$ cores, up to $k$ threads can be *élu* simultaneously.
3. **Bloqué (*Waiting / Blocked*):** Suspended while waiting for an event—for example, `PcoSemaphore::acquire()`, `PcoMutex::lock()`, `PcoThread::join()`, `sleep()`, or an I/O operation.
4. **Zombie:** The thread has finished executing, but its creator/parent has not yet collected its termination via `join()` (*jointure*).
5. **Terminé (*Terminated*):** Pseudo-state where resources are freed and the thread disappears.

blocks.title: Thread State Transition Diagram
blocks.caption: Note the two paths out of 'élu': normal/blocking wait ('attente -> bloqué -> réveil -> prêt') and termination ('terminaison -> zombie -> jointure -> terminé').
blocks.source:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> pret : création
  pret --> elu : exécution
  elu --> pret : préemption
  elu --> bloque : attente (I/O, mutex, sémaphore, join)
  bloque --> pret : réveil
  elu --> termine : terminaison (détaché)
  elu --> zombie : terminaison
  zombie --> termine : jointure (join)

blocks.title: Green Threads vs. Native Threads
blocks.content:
* **Green Thread:** Scheduled in user space by a virtual machine or runtime library that emulates an OS scheduler (useful on bare-metal systems without an OS). Cannot exploit multiple CPU cores on its own.
* **Native Thread:** Managed and scheduled directly by the OS kernel. **This is the only way to exploit multi-core parallelism.** Both C++ (`std::thread`, `PcoThread`) and modern Java use native threads.

### Context Switch Sequence
1. Move the active thread to the **ready** (if preempted) or **blocked** (if waiting) queue.
2. **Save** its execution context (`PC`, `SP`, CPU registers).
3. **Select** the highest-priority eligible thread from the ready queue.
4. **Restore** the chosen thread's saved execution context.
5. **Activate** the chosen thread—from its perspective, it never noticed the interruption.

sections.title: 3. The PcoThread C++ API
sections.description: Creating threads, passing arguments safely, joining, and cooperative cancellation.

blocks.title: Creating Threads & Passing Arguments

annotations.note: Arguments are copied by value by default; references require std::ref().
First argument is &Class::method, second is the object pointer (obj or this), followed by method arguments.

blocks.title: Joining & Cooperative Termination
blocks.content:
* **`join()`:** Blocks the calling thread until the target thread finishes. Also prevents the main thread from returning early and killing the whole process!
* **Self-termination (`return;`):** Cleanly ends the thread and wakes any thread blocked on `join()`. Note: returning from `main()` terminates the **entire process** and all its threads.
* **Cooperative Cancellation (`requestStop()` / `stopRequested()`):** Never forcefully kill another thread—it could leave shared data structures or mutexes in an inconsistent state. Instead:
  1. Caller invokes `thread->requestStop();`
  2. Worker periodically checks `if (PcoThread::thisThread()->stopRequested()) return;`
  3. Caller waits with `thread->join();`

> [!WARNING]
> **Lifetime Trap:** To call `thread->requestStop()`, the `PcoThread` object must still exist and be initialized! Also, if `t1` calls `t2->requestStop()` before `t2` is assigned in `main()`, you have a null-pointer race condition.

blocks.title: Passing References to PcoThread
blocks.front: Why must you wrap a reference argument in `std::ref(x)` when constructing a `PcoThread`, and what is the lifetime danger?
blocks.back:
`PcoThread`'s constructor copies arguments **by value** by default (like `std::thread`). `std::ref(x)` creates a `std::reference_wrapper` so the thread function receives a true reference.

**Danger:** If `x` lives on the creator's stack and the creator exits its scope before the spawned thread finishes, the reference becomes **dangling** (undefined behavior).
blocks.hint: Think about template argument forwarding and stack frame lifetimes.

blocks.concept: Thread vs. Process Memory & Cooperative Cancellation
blocks.prompt: Explain why two threads in the same process can corrupt each other's global variables even though each has its own local variables, and why we use requestStop()/stopRequested() instead of forcefully killing a thread.

Forceful termination leaves shared state/locks corrupted
Cooperative cancellation lets the thread exit at a safe point

blocks.question: Each thread within a process possesses:
options: An address space shared among all threads of the same process
An address space shared among all threads on the operating system
Only a shared stack, while heap memory is private per thread
blocks.correct_answer: An address space shared among all threads of the same process
blocks.explanation: All threads of the same process share the process's address space (Text and Data/Heap segments). Each thread only has its own private stack and execution context (PC, registers). Threads of different processes do not share an address space.
hints: Recall the three segments of a process: Text, Data/Heap, and Stack.
How do threads of the same process communicate so easily compared to separate processes?

blocks.question: On a single-core processor (monocœur), how many threads can be simultaneously in the 'élu' (running) state?
options: As many threads as exist in the process
blocks.explanation: A single CPU core can execute at most one instruction stream at any instant (max 1). If all threads are blocked waiting for I/O or synchronization, 0 threads are in the running state (min 0).
hints: How many instruction streams can a single core execute at the exact same nanosecond?
What if every thread in the system is currently blocked on sleep() or I/O?

blocks.question: In a `PcoThread` worker loop, a developer writes `if (PcoThread::thisThread()->stopRequested()) { std::cout << "Stopping"; }` inside a helper function `checkStop()`, without returning from the worker loop. What happens when `requestStop()` is called?
options: The worker thread prints "Stopping" and keeps running forever because `return` only exits `checkStop()`, not the worker loop.
The worker thread immediately terminates because `stopRequested()` throws a cancellation exception.
The main thread's `join()` unblocks as soon as `requestStop()` is called.
The OS kernel preempts and destroys the worker thread.
blocks.correct_answer: The worker thread prints "Stopping" and keeps running forever because `return` only exits `checkStop()`, not the worker loop.
blocks.explanation: `requestStop()` only sets a boolean flag on the target `PcoThread`. It does not interrupt or kill the thread. If `checkStop()` returns `void` and only `return`s from itself, the caller's `for`/`while` loop continues executing!
hints: Does `requestStop()` force-kill a thread, or is it purely cooperative?
If a helper function `void should_stop()` executes `return;`, which function does it return from?
